column4: ch-009 chunk 1 (Lwanga-Lunyiigo and Vansina, Bantu languages)
column5: The Bantu family has over 400 languages from one ancestor, proven by regular sound and grammar correspondences (proto-Bantu glossary of over 500 roots); origin: Greenberg's Benue-Cross west placement is 'now accepted as accurate by all linguists' per this 1988 chapter (three independent studies since 1973 showed Guthrie's Shaba centre wrong) and Oliver has abandoned his four-phase theory; Western and Eastern blocs, the Eastern bloc more closely related so it expanded later and faster; there is still no accepted genealogical tree because of convergence (borrowing). Crucially the chapter warns against assuming language spread equals mass migration: Romance, Sekyani/Mpongwe, Afrikaans show language shift; 'it is misguided to speak in terms of massive population movements' given low densities. The course's Grollemund line (tree from 2015) fits. Module 1: state 'Bantu languages spread from the Cameroon-Nigeria borderland; how far by migration vs language shift is debated' [CONTESTED].

column4: ch-009 chunk 2 (Bantu: dating, causes, and archaeology)
column5: The chapter dates proto-Bantu between about 1000 BCE or earlier and 400 BCE (a Neolithic community with cereals and yam, only goat, fishing speciality, no metal), the expansion took 2,000-3,000 years and reached the east coast by the 8th century; it rejects both the 'population explosion' (Posnansky) and the 'iron conquest' (Wrigley) theories as too dramatic: agriculture and iron spread gradually, iron arrowheads were not clearly better than stone for long; expansion was 'small numbers of people from one village to the next', often changing direction, not an exodus; archaeology cannot prove which language the makers spoke (Urewe pottery link is coincidence-risk), and the rapid spread of iron could be the work of a minority of smiths and potters; no trace of autochthonous languages remains in the western Bantu zone, explained by village living and fishermen's contacts; Rwanda furnaces dated +32, +255, +380 (calendar). Module 1: replace the migration-wave story with this slower village-to-village model and say iron/pottery do not equal language [CONTESTED].

Ehret's account (eastern proto-Bantu west of Lake Tanganyika, Pela and Pembele spreading in the first centuries CE) has not been followed up by linguists, 'the evidence is too slender'; the chapter concludes that origin and cause of the expansion cannot yet be stated, and warns that 'Bantu' is a linguistic label, not a people, culture or philosophy: a 'Bantu myth' could grow like the Hamitic myth. An Editor's note records that coauthor Lwanga-Lunyiigo disagrees with most specialists and denies any movement from West Africa (his 1976 view) citing Negroid remains at Iwo Eleru (about 9250 BCE), Asselar, Ishango; the editors print this dissent separately. Module 1: present the West African origin as the mainstream linguistic view, with the dissent noted, plus the 'label not people' warning [CONTESTED].

Almoravids grew from the veiled Sanhadja of the Western Sahara (Massufa, Lamtuna, Judala), after a century of disunity, loss of the salt and gold trade termini (Sijilmasa, Awdaghust) to Zanata and Ifriqiyan traders after 970, and a new salt mine at Taghaza that broke the Awlil monopoly; Ibn Yasin's career is thinly known (chronology 'uncertain and confused', al-Bakri doubted his learning but was biased against Saharan Berbers); first phase among the Judala from about 1039 to 1053, expelled, then the Lamtuna became the mainstay; the chapter links the movement to a Maliki revival at Kairouan. Module 3: the Almoravids began as a Saharan reform movement tied to trade routes, not a sudden conquest [PROBABLE].

The old reading of 'al-Murabitun' as 'people of the ribat (fortress)' rests on one late source (Ibn Abi Zar, after 1326) and is abandoned by recent scholarship (Norris, Moraes Farias, Levtzion, Meier); the 1966 IFAN dig on Tidra island found no ribat and no clay or stone to build one, so the name is read as dedication to jihad or to 'the bond'; Ibn Yasin died 1059 fighting the Barghawata; Marrakesh was founded 463/1070 not 454/1062 (revised after Levi-Provencal, Huici Miranda, Deverdun); Abu Bakr handed command to cousin Yusuf ibn Tashfin about 1072 and Yusuf had Fez in 1075, Ceuta in 1083, crossed to Spain in 1086 and won at Zallaqa (Sagrajas). Yusuf bought black slaves from the Sudan and Christian captives for his army. Module 3: teach the name and Marrakesh date as revised [PROBABLE].

The chapter does not state that the Almoravids conquered Ghana in 1076: it says archaeology is 'still vague' (destruction traces deep down at Koumbi Saleh, mosque dimensions changed after the 11th century, the town peaked in the 13th-14th centuries), 'conclusive proof is still lacking', cites Conrad and Fisher's 1982-83 arguments against the presupposed conquest, and says a raid would not have ended the market town. It says Ghana 'officially went over to Islam at the end of the fifth/eleventh century'. This contrasts with Niane's vol. IV chapter (Koumbi fell 1076). Module 4 and 3: present the 1076 fall as one view and the conquest as unproven [CONTESTED]. Islam in the Sahel pre-dated the Almoravids: Takrur's chief Labi was with Abu Bakr in 1056, Soninke merchants may have brought Islam by the ninth-tenth century (Kane), Gao's princes were Muslim by the tenth century and the Gao-Sane stelae may be Spanish marble.

column4: ch-016 chunk 3 (Almoravid conquest of Spain; Senegal valley)
column5: Almoravids crossed to Spain in 1086 at the call of al-Mutamid of Seville, won at Zallaqa, then annexed Muslim Spain by 1094 (Toledo and Saragossa excepted); the empire ran from the Ebro to the Senegal. Senegal valley: Sintiu-Bara a big site by the 5th-6th centuries, Ogo smelted iron in the 9th, Silla and Takrur dominated the middle river; Ba (1984) hypothesises early iron-producer dynasties; much of this is hypothesis. Almoravids gave West African Islam 'a geographical dimension', and the first organised conversion effort was theirs in the 11th century. Module 3.

Economic unity from Ebro to Senegal: gold flowed north and Spanish-minted dinars south (found in Mauritania), two armies (camel in the south, horse in the north), Aghmat merchants rich on the Sudan trade (al-Idrisi), Marrakesh built of clay and baked brick with the first palace and fountain excavated; the Maliki jurists' severity (al-Ghazali's books burned about 1143), weak local administration (power through relatives and clients), and the Atlas-based Almohad movement brought it down; the chapter says history has been 'far too hard' on the Almoravids and the earlier idea that their conquests devastated the Sahel is wrong. Abu Bakr's death date varies 462/1069 to 480/1087 in the sources. Module 3.
